Quavo has released *QRÖMELIFE*, his third solo album and the follow-up to 2023's *Rocket Power*. That record stayed close to the grief after Takeoff's death. The new album still carries his nephew's absence, but it leaves more room for the rest of his life, including his reconciliation with Offset and the arrival of his daughter.

The title comes from the word "qrome," which he says is connected to "chromosome." He uses it to describe what happens after something difficult becomes part of you but daily life keeps going. His example is simple: a person can suffer a loss and still have to wake up and go to work the next morning. That is also how the record treats Takeoff's death. It remains part of the album, but other subjects now have more room.

Working with Pharrell Williams pulled him back toward the melodic side of his voice. In interviews about the album, he has talked about recovering the flexibility that let him move between Migos records, solo singles and pop features without sounding trapped in one mode. "Trance (Walk It Down)" is one of the clearest examples, with a looser delivery than the heavier material on *Rocket Power*. Other tracks return to harder drums and sharper rhythms, so the melodic side is only one part of the record.

[apple:album:6809921222]

"Away" reunites him with Offset on record after the split that fractured Migos before Takeoff's death. The two later repaired their relationship. He described the session as therapeutic and compared it to being back in the school cafeteria with someone he has known since seventh grade. They are also sorting through new Migos music. Any future release under the group name, he has said, would need to honor Takeoff and benefit his estate rather than simply present Migos as a duo.

Fatherhood gives the album a subject that did not exist on *Rocket Power*. He is now a father to a daughter, and he has spoken about the role in relation to his own childhood. His father died when he was four. He says he wants to be present for the parts of his daughter's life that he never had a father there to see. The short film released with *QRÖMELIFE* moves through old Migos footage, Takeoff, recent studio sessions and the years that followed before ending with him holding his daughter. Fatherhood, not grief, is the last image the film leaves behind.
